events.title: Early Maya Settlement
events.description: Maya people began settling in present-day Guatemala, establishing agricultural communities. Early settlements included Pacific coast and highland regions. Maya cultivated maize, beans and squash, developing complex agricultural techniques. This marked beginning of Maya civilization, with Guatemala becoming heartland of Maya world.

events.title: Early Preclassic Period
events.description: Maya civilization entered Early Preclassic period, beginning construction of permanent villages and early ceremonial centers. Pottery making developed, early social hierarchies emerged. Early cities like Nakbe began rising. Maya hieroglyphic writing system began developing.

events.title: El Mirador Rise
events.description: El Mirador became one of largest Maya cities, with massive pyramid architecture. La Danta pyramid is one of largest structures in pre-Columbian Americas, exceeding Great Pyramid of Giza in volume. El Mirador demonstrated early Maya civilization's architectural and organizational capabilities.

events.title: Kaminaljuyu Prosperity
events.description: Kaminaljuyu became major city in Guatemalan highlands, located in present-day Guatemala City. City controlled obsidian trade, important material for tools and weapons. Kaminaljuyu developed complex social structure and trade networks, with connections to Teotihuacan in Mexico.

events.title: Maya Calendar Perfection
events.description: Maya perfected complex calendar system, including 260-day sacred calendar (Tzolk'in) and 365-day solar calendar (Haab'). Long Count calendar recorded historical events. Maya astronomers precisely calculated planetary movements and eclipses. This calendar system was most accurate in pre-Columbian Americas.

events.title: Capital Destruction
events.description: Agua volcano eruption triggered mudslide, destroying Ciudad Vieja capital, killing hundreds including Alvarado's widow. Survivors decided to establish new capital in nearby Panchoy Valley. This disaster viewed as divine punishment for Spanish conquest brutality.

events.title: Classic Period Beginning
events.description: Maya civilization entered Classic period, city-state system formed. Tikal began rising as major power center. Monument carving and hieroglyphic writing system matured. Maya art, architecture and science reached peaks. This was beginning of Maya civilization's golden age.

events.title: Tikal Expansion
events.description: Tikal became one of most powerful Maya city-states in lowlands, controlling vast territory and trade routes. Tikal's rulers built massive pyramids and palaces. City population reached tens of thousands. Tikal warred and allied with other city-states like Uaxactun.

events.title: Teotihuacan Conquest of Tikal
events.description: General Siyaj K'ak' from central Mexican Teotihuacan conquered Tikal, establishing new dynasty. Teotihuacan influence introduced new architectural styles, weapons and rituals. This conquest changed power balance in Peten region, Tikal reorganized under foreign rule.

events.title: Copan Rise
events.description: Copan (in modern Honduras but part of Maya cultural sphere) became important cultural center of southeastern Maya region. Copan famous for exquisite carvings, hieroglyphic stairway and astronomical observatory. Copan's rulers patronized arts and sciences, making it Athens of Maya civilization.

events.title: Quirigua Founded
events.description: Quirigua established in Motagua River valley, initially vassal state of Copan. Quirigua controlled important jade and obsidian trade routes. City later became famous for massive stelae, including tallest stela in Maya world.

events.title: Peten City-States Flourishing
events.description: Numerous Maya city-states in Peten region reached prosperity peak, including Tikal, Calakmul, Naranjo and Yaxha. City-states engaged in complex diplomacy, trade and warfare. Maya hieroglyphics recorded dynastic histories, conquests and rituals.

events.title: Tikal Defeated by Calakmul
events.description: Calakmul and its ally Caracol defeated Tikal, causing Tikal to enter decline period of 130 years without erecting stelae. This called Tikal's 'dark period.' Calakmul became dominant force in Peten region, forming 'Snake Kingdom' alliance against Tikal.

events.title: Maya Art Zenith
events.description: Late Classic Maya art reached zenith, including exquisite murals (like Bonampak), pottery, jade objects and carvings. Maya writing system widely used to record history, astronomy and religious knowledge. Maya architecture reached complexity, including vaulted ceilings, palaces and ball courts.

events.title: Tikal Revival
events.description: Under ruler Jasaw Chan K'awiil I, Tikal defeated longtime rival Calakmul, beginning revival. Tikal built Temple I (Jasaw Chan K'awiil I's tomb) and other magnificent structures. Tikal regained dominance in Peten region.

events.title: Quirigua Defeats Copan
events.description: Quirigua king K'ak' Tiliw Chan Yopaat defeated and captured Copan king Uaxaclajuun Ub'aah K'awiil in Motagua valley. Copan king was executed, major event in Maya history. Quirigua gained independence from Copan, beginning its golden age.

events.title: Highland Maya Culture
events.description: Maya cities in Guatemalan highlands like Iximche, Q'umarkaj and Mixco Viejo flourished. Highland Maya included K'iche', Kaqchikel, Mam and Tz'utujil groups. They developed distinctive culture blending lowland and highland traditions.

events.title: Classic Period Collapse Begins
events.description: Southern Maya lowland city-states began collapsing, many cities abandoned. Causes possibly included drought, overpopulation, environmental degradation, warfare and social unrest. Stela erection stopped, palaces and temples abandoned. This most mysterious event in Maya history, called 'Classic Period Collapse.'

events.title: Piedras Negras Abandoned
events.description: Piedras Negras was among first major cities abandoned. Last stela dated 810 CE. City's ruling class disappeared, commoners gradually left. This marked end of Maya civilization in Usumacinta River region.

events.title: Copan Decline
events.description: Copan entered final decline phase, dynasty ended. Last rulers unable to maintain city's population and economy. Copan's artistic and architectural activities stopped. By late 9th century, Copan almost completely abandoned, jungle swallowing palaces and temples.

events.title: Quirigua Abandoned
events.description: Quirigua followed other southern lowland cities into decline. Last stela dated around 810 CE. By mid-9th century, city largely abandoned. Quirigua's massive stelae became silent witnesses of deserted city until 19th century rediscovery.

events.title: Tikal Abandoned
events.description: One of Maya's greatest cities Tikal finally abandoned. Palaces and temples abandoned, jungle swallowed plazas. Tikal's last stela dated 869 CE. This marked end of Classic Period Maya civilization in Peten region. Tikal's ruins slept in jungle for nearly millennium.

events.title: Postclassic Period Begins
events.description: Maya civilization entered Postclassic period, power centers shifted from southern lowlands to northern Yucatan Peninsula and Guatemalan highlands. Central Mexican Toltec culture influenced Maya region. Militarism increased, new art styles emerged. Guatemalan highland cities continued flourishing.

events.title: Highland City-States Competition
events.description: Guatemalan highlands formed multiple competing Maya city-states, including K'iche', Kaqchikel, Mam and Tz'utujil kingdoms. These kingdoms fought over territory, trade routes and resources. Highland Maya culture blended Classic period traditions with Postclassic militarism.

events.title: K'iche' Kingdom Rise
events.description: K'iche' kingdom became dominant force in western Guatemalan highlands. K'iche' people established capital Q'umarkaj (called Utatlán by Spanish). K'iche' kingdom expanded through conquest and alliance, becoming most powerful highland kingdom before Spanish arrival. K'iche' culture preserved in Popol Vuh.

events.title: Kaqchikel Split
events.description: Kaqchikel people split from K'iche' kingdom, establishing independent kingdom. This caused longtime enmity between two kingdoms. Kaqchikel people founded important city Iximche, becoming rival force to K'iche'.

events.title: Iximche Founded
events.description: Kaqchikel people established capital Iximche in strategic highland location. Iximche had palaces, temples and ball courts, well-fortified. City became center of Kaqchikel power, controlling important trade routes. Iximche played important role in Spanish conquest.

events.title: K'iche' Empire Expansion
events.description: Under ruler Quicab, K'iche' kingdom reached maximum expansion, controlling most Guatemalan highlands. K'iche' conquered neighboring Maya groups, establishing tribute system. Q'umarkaj became major political and religious center with magnificent temples and palaces.

events.title: K'iche'-Kaqchikel Wars
events.description: Long wars erupted between K'iche' and Kaqchikel kingdoms, weakening both kingdoms' power. Wars mainly over territory and trade control. This division later exploited by Spanish conquistadors using divide-and-rule strategy.

events.title: Guatemala on Eve of Spanish Arrival
events.description: Before Spanish arrival, Guatemala was home to multiple Maya kingdoms including K'iche', Kaqchikel, Mam, Tz'utujil. Estimated population reached several million. Maya had complex societies, developed agriculture, trade networks and rich culture. But divisions between kingdoms made them vulnerable to foreign conquest.

events.title: Cortés Passes Through
events.description: Spanish expedition led by Hernán Cortés possibly passed through Guatemalan border regions en route to Mexico. News of Cortés's conquest of Aztec Empire reached Maya region, causing alarm. Some Maya envoys traveled to Mexico to observe Spanish power.

events.title: Alvarado Expedition Preparation
events.description: Cortés sent Pedro de Alvarado to lead expedition conquering Guatemala. Alvarado was brutal but effective conquistador who participated in Mexico conquest. He led about 300 Spanish soldiers and thousands of Mexican indigenous allies, equipped with horses, firearms and steel weapons.

events.title: Conquest of Tz'utujil and Mam
events.description: Alvarado continued conquering other Maya kingdoms. Tz'utujil people resisted around Lake Atitlán, many warriors choosing to jump into lake rather than surrender. Mam kingdom in western highlands also fiercely resisted. Spanish brutal repression caused thousands of Maya deaths.

events.title: Spanish Invasion Begins
events.description: Alvarado led expedition from Mexico into Guatemala, beginning conquest. Spanish first encountered Maya in Soconusco region. Spanish horses, firearms and steel weapons shocked Maya. Alvarado used brutal methods including burning villages and executing resistant chiefs.

events.title: Battle of Xelajú
events.description: Spanish army fought first major battle with K'iche' Maya army at Xelajú. K'iche' warriors fought bravely but couldn't withstand Spanish cavalry and firearms. K'iche' legendary warrior Tecún Umán fell in battle, becoming symbol of Maya resistance. Spanish gained decisive victory, opening way for conquest.

events.title: Fall of Q'umarkaj
events.description: Alvarado attacked K'iche' capital Q'umarkaj. When K'iche' chiefs tried ambushing Spanish inside city, Alvarado discovered plot, captured and executed K'iche' rulers. Spanish burned Q'umarkaj, destroying temples and palaces. This marked end of K'iche' kingdom, turning point in Guatemalan history.

events.title: Alliance with Kaqchikel
events.description: Alvarado allied with K'iche's enemy Kaqchikel kingdom. Kaqchikel offered their capital Iximche to Spanish as base. This 'divide-and-rule' strategy crucial to Spanish conquest. Kaqchikel hoped to use Spanish power against K'iche', but soon realized mistake.

events.title: Santiago de los Caballeros Founded
events.description: Alvarado founded first Spanish capital 'Santiago de los Caballeros' near Iximche. This marked official beginning of Spanish colonial Guatemala. City became base for further Spanish conquest of Central America. July 25 (St. James Day) became important date for Guatemala.

events.title: Kaqchikel Rebellion
events.description: Kaqchikel people rebelled due to excessive Spanish demands for gold and slaves. They abandoned Iximche, retreating to mountains for guerrilla warfare. Spanish lost main ally and capital. Kaqchikel rebellion lasted years, complicating Spanish conquest.

events.title: Capital Relocation
events.description: Due to continued war with Kaqchikel, Spanish moved capital from Iximche to Almolonga valley (Ciudad Vieja). New capital located in fertile valley at volcano's foot. This was second location of Santiago de los Caballeros.

events.title: Colonial Government Established
events.description: Spanish established colonial government structure in Guatemala, including municipal council and royal officials. Alvarado appointed Governor of Guatemala. Spanish began implementing encomienda system, assigning Maya communities to Spanish conquistadors, forcing them to provide labor and tribute.

events.title: Peten Conquest Attempts
events.description: Spanish made multiple attempts conquering independent Maya kingdoms in Peten lowlands, including Itza people's Tayasal. But jungle environment, disease and Maya resistance caused conquest failures. Peten remained independent over 150 years, becoming last bastion of Maya resistance.

events.title: Kaqchikel Surrender
events.description: After five years of guerrilla warfare, Kaqchikel people finally surrendered to Spanish. Continued warfare, starvation and disease weakened resistance. Kaqchikel leaders reached peace agreement with Spanish. Iximche was abandoned, Kaqchikel people forced to resettle in Spanish-controlled villages.

events.title: Antigua Guatemala Founded
events.description: Spanish established third and most enduring capital in Panchoy Valley, called Santiago de Guatemala (today's Antigua Guatemala). City planned according to Spanish grid pattern, with cathedral, palaces and monasteries. Antigua became one of most important colonial cities in Central America, serving as capital of Captaincy General of Guatemala.

events.title: New Laws Promulgated
events.description: Spanish King Charles V promulgated New Laws attempting to reform encomienda system and protect indigenous people. Laws prohibited indigenous slavery and limited conquistador power. But in Guatemala, these laws strongly resisted, rarely enforced. Spanish settlers continued exploiting Maya labor.

events.title: Captaincy General of Guatemala Established
events.description: Spanish formally established Captaincy General of Guatemala, with jurisdiction from Chiapas (modern Mexico) to Costa Rica, encompassing all Central America. Antigua Guatemala became capital. Captaincy General reported directly to Viceroy of New Spain, later directly to Spanish King. This established Guatemala's position as Central America's political center for nearly 300 years.

events.title: Royal Audiencia of Antigua
events.description: Spanish established Royal Audiencia (Real Audiencia) in Antigua, Central America's supreme court and administrative body. Audiencia composed of judges, handling legal cases and overseeing colonial officials. This strengthened Spanish control over Central America, making Antigua true colonial power center.

events.title: Catholic Evangelization
events.description: Catholic Church began large-scale evangelization activities, converting Maya to Christianity. Dominican, Franciscan and other orders established monasteries and churches. Missionaries learned Maya languages and compiled grammars and dictionaries. Forced conversion often accompanied suppression of Maya religion, but many Maya blended Catholicism with traditional beliefs, forming distinctive syncretic religion.

events.title: Congregation System Implementation
events.description: Spanish implemented 'congregation' (reducción) policy, concentrating scattered Maya communities into newly established 'congregation villages' (pueblos de indios). This made Spanish control, taxation and evangelization easier. Maya forced to leave traditional settlements, disrupting social structures. But some Maya used these villages to preserve their culture and languages.

events.title: Popol Vuh Recorded
events.description: K'iche' Maya nobles recorded Popol Vuh using Latin alphabet, important text of Maya creation myth and history. Text recorded K'iche' origins, Hero Twins' adventures and K'iche' dynastic history. Popol Vuh became one of most important documents understanding pre-Columbian Maya culture, called 'Maya Bible.'

events.title: Plague Pandemic
events.description: Devastating plague (possibly typhus or measles) struck Guatemala, killing estimated half of indigenous population. European diseases had catastrophic impact on Maya without immunity. Population collapse made Spanish control of survivors easier, transforming economic and social structures.

events.title: Indigo Cultivation Expansion
events.description: Indigo dye became Guatemala's main export commodity. Indigo in high demand for European textile industry. Spanish landowners established large indigo plantations on Pacific coast, forcing Maya to labor. Indigo production conditions harsh, many workers died from toxic fumes and overwork. But indigo brought enormous wealth to colonial elites.

events.title: Antigua's Golden Age
events.description: Antigua Guatemala entered golden age, becoming one of most beautiful colonial cities in Spanish America. Magnificent churches, monasteries, palaces and universities built. City attracted artists, architects and scholars. Antigua's Baroque architecture blended Spanish, Moorish and indigenous elements. City became Central America's cultural and religious center.

events.title: University of San Carlos Founded
events.description: University of San Carlos founded in Antigua, Central America's third oldest university. University provided theology, law, medicine and arts education. San Carlos became colonial intellectual training center, later playing important role in independence movement. University trained many of Guatemala's leaders and thinkers.

events.title: Black Christ of Esquipulas
events.description: Black Christ statue of Esquipulas became Central America's most important pilgrimage site. Legend said this black wooden crucifix had miraculous healing powers. Tens of thousands of pilgrims annually traveled to Esquipulas, including Spanish, Mestizos and Maya. Black Christ worship blended Catholic and pre-Spanish religious elements, becoming symbol of Guatemalan religious identity.

events.title: Fall of Tayasal
events.description: Spanish army under Martín de Ursúa conquered Itza Maya capital Tayasal (modern Flores), ending last independent Maya kingdom in Peten. This marked final completion of Spanish conquest of Maya, 173 years after Alvarado began conquest. Itza king Kan Ek' surrendered, Peten incorporated into Spanish Empire. This one of longest records of indigenous American resistance to European conquest.

events.title: Earthquake Damage
events.description: Strong earthquake severely damaged Antigua Guatemala, destroying many buildings and churches. Earthquake killed hundreds. City began reconstruction, but earthquake disasters became norm for Antigua's history due to location in seismically active volcanic zone.

events.title: Cacao and Coffee Introduction
events.description: Guatemala began growing cacao and early coffee crops, which would become major export commodities in 19th century. Pacific coast and highland climates ideally suited for coffee cultivation. Spanish landowners established large farms (haciendas), relying on forced Maya labor. This laid foundation for Guatemala's agricultural export economy, continuing to modern times.

events.title: Colonial Social Hierarchy
events.description: Guatemala developed strict racial and social hierarchy system. Top tier was Peninsulares (Spanish-born Spaniards), then Criollos (American-born Spaniards), Mestizos (mixed race), Mulatos (Spanish-African mixed), indigenous and African slaves. This caste system determined legal rights, occupational choices and social status. Indigenous were largest group but most oppressed, excluded from political power and bearing heavy taxes and labor obligations.

events.title: Santa Marta Earthquake
events.description: Catastrophic Santa Marta earthquakes destroyed Antigua Guatemala, causing widespread destruction and thousands of deaths. Aftershocks continued for months, making city uninhabitable. Cathedral, palaces and monasteries became ruins. This earthquake changed Guatemalan history, forcing capital relocation. Survivors debated whether to rebuild or move to new location.

events.title: Capital Moved to New Guatemala
events.description: After debate, Spanish authorities decided to move capital from destroyed Antigua to new location in Ermita Valley (Valle de la Ermita), called 'New Guatemala' (Nueva Guatemala de la Asunción), today's Guatemala City. New city designed according to Enlightenment rational planning, with wide streets and plazas. Many residents reluctant to leave Antigua, causing conflict. Antigua abandoned, becoming 'Old' Guatemala (Antigua).

events.title: Enlightenment Ideas Spread
events.description: Enlightenment ideas began spreading among Guatemala's Criollo elites, mainly through University of San Carlos. Intellectuals read works of Rousseau, Voltaire and Locke, discussing natural rights, liberty and political reform. These ideas laid intellectual foundation for later independence movement. But Spanish authorities tried censoring 'dangerous' ideas, seeing them as threatening colonial order.

events.title: Impact of Napoleon's Spain Invasion
events.description: Napoleon's invasion of Spain and deposition of King Ferdinand VII triggered crisis in Guatemala and throughout Spanish America. Colonial authorities faced legitimacy question: who had right to rule? Guatemala elites began discussing autonomy or even independence. Conservatives supported maintaining ties with Spain, while liberals pushed for reform and greater autonomy. Tensions increased, paving way for 1821 independence.

events.title: Early Independence Conspiracies
events.description: Several early independence conspiracies emerged in Guatemala, including 1811 Belen Conspiracy. Liberal Criollos, priests and intellectuals secretly plotted to overthrow Spanish rule. But conspiracies discovered, leaders arrested. Spanish authorities strengthened repression, but couldn't stop spread of independence ideas. These early attempts created conditions for final independence in 1821.

events.title: Spanish Liberal Constitution
events.description: Spain's liberal revolution restored 1812 Constitution, granting colonies more autonomy and representation. Guatemala elected representatives to Spanish Parliament. Liberal reforms inspired Guatemala's liberals, but also provoked conservative Church and landowner opposition. Constitution's brief implementation showed autonomy possibilities, accelerating independence movement.

events.title: Guatemalan Independence
events.description: Guatemala and all Central America declared independence from Spain after meeting in Guatemala City. Independence led by conservative elites hoping to maintain control after Mexico's independence. Independence declaration achieved in relative peace, without warfare. Gabino Gainza became provisional government head. But Central America's future after independence remained uncertain, sparking debate about joining Mexico or forming independent federation. September 15 became Independence Day for Guatemala and Central America.

events.title: Annexation to Mexican Empire
events.description: Guatemala and most of Central America annexed into Agustín de Iturbide's First Mexican Empire. Conservatives supported annexation, hoping empire would protect traditional order. But liberals and many provinces (like El Salvador) opposed, preferring independent federation. Annexation was controversial and short-lived. Many Central Americans saw this as betrayal of independence.

events.title: Central American Federation Founded
events.description: After Iturbide's Mexican Empire collapsed, Central American provinces formed United Provinces of Central America (Central American Federation), including Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, Nicaragua and Costa Rica. Federation adopted liberal constitution, establishing federal republic system. Guatemala City became capital. But from beginning, Federation plagued by regionalism, ideological conflict between liberals and conservatives, and economic difficulties.

events.title: Slavery Abolished
events.description: Central American Federation abolished slavery, becoming one of first regions in Americas to do so. Though Guatemala's slave population relatively small (mainly African descendants in coastal areas), this was important liberal reform. Abolition reflected Federation's commitment to Enlightenment ideas and human rights.

events.title: Manuel José Arce President
events.description: Manuel José Arce elected first President of Central American Federation. Arce initially liberal, but after taking office aligned with conservatives, trying to strengthen central power. This provoked liberal opposition, leading to civil war. Arce's betrayal viewed as first major blow to Federation stability.

events.title: Central American Civil War
events.description: Federal civil war erupted between liberals and conservatives. Liberals led by Francisco Morazán, conservatives supported by President Arce and Guatemala elites. War spread across republics, killing thousands. In 1829, Morazán defeated conservatives, captured Guatemala City, becoming liberal hero.

events.title: Morazán Reforms
events.description: Francisco Morazán became Federation's power figure (later elected president), implementing radical liberal reforms. Reforms included weakening Church power, confiscating Church property, introducing jury trials, promoting education and religious freedom. Morazán tried to build secular progressive state. But reforms threatened conservative elites, Church and traditional communities, provoking strong opposition.

events.title: Church Property Confiscation
events.description: Liberal government confiscated Catholic Church property, including land, monasteries and church assets. This aimed to weaken Church's political and economic power, and finance state. But confiscation angered conservatives and devout Catholics (including many Maya). Church became staunch opponent of liberal regime, contributing to 1830s rebellions.

events.title: Cholera Epidemic and Rebellion
events.description: Cholera epidemic struck Guatemala, killing thousands. Rumors spread that government deliberately poisoned water. Liberal reforms, forced vaccination and Church persecution triggered mass peasant rebellion. Maya communities, conservatives and Church-backed peasant uprising opposed liberal government. Rebellion led by Rafael Carrera, Mestizo pig herder who became conservative leader.

events.title: Rafael Carrera Rise
events.description: Rafael Carrera led conservative peasant army capturing Guatemala City. Carrera was charismatic leader supported by Maya peasants, conservative elites and Church. He overthrew liberal government, restored Church privileges, abolished liberal reforms. Carrera became Guatemala's most powerful figure, ruling for 25 years.

events.title: Central American Federation Dissolution
events.description: Central American Federation dissolved under pressure of civil war, economic crisis and regionalism. Each republic declared complete independence. Guatemala under Carrera withdrew first. Morazán tried to save Federation but failed, executed in 1842. Federation dissolution ended dream of Central American unity. Five nations went separate ways, but unity idea continued influencing Central American politics.

events.title: Republic of Guatemala Declared
events.description: Rafael Carrera formally declared Guatemala as independent sovereign republic. Guatemala adopted conservative constitution, granting Carrera broad powers. Carrera declared 'President for Life,' essentially dictator. He restored Church's central position, abolished liberal reforms, established authoritarian conservative regime.

events.title: Carrera Conservative Rule
events.description: Carrera consolidated conservative rule, becoming Central America's most powerful figure. He intervened in neighboring countries supporting conservatives against liberals. Carrera restored Church property, signed concordat with Holy See. He maintained social order but suppressed political opposition. Carrera's rule brought stability but at cost of liberty and progress. He viewed as savior by conservatives, tyrant by liberals.

events.title: War with El Salvador
events.description: Guatemala waged war with liberal El Salvador and Honduras, Carrera trying to install friendly regimes in neighboring countries. War attracted US and Mexican mediation. This demonstrated Guatemala's military dominance in Central America. Carrera became protector of regional conservatism, intervening in neighbors against liberal regimes.

events.title: Belize Treaty with Britain
events.description: Guatemala signed treaty with Britain recognizing British sovereignty over British Honduras (modern Belize), in exchange for British promise to build road connecting Guatemala City to Caribbean Sea. Road never built, Guatemala later declared treaty void. Belize territorial dispute became longtime issue in Guatemalan politics, remaining unresolved into 21st century.

events.title: Rafael Carrera Death
events.description: Rafael Carrera died after ruling Guatemala for 25 years, leaving power vacuum. Carrera's death marked end of conservative rule era. Successor Vicente Cerna couldn't maintain Carrera's authority. Liberals saw opportunity to seize power, began plotting revolution.

events.title: Liberal Revolution
events.description: Liberals led by Miguel García Granados and Justo Rufino Barrios launched revolution, overthrowing conservative government. Rebellion started from Mexican border, supported by peasants and urban liberals. On June 30, 1871, liberals captured Guatemala City, ending conservative rule era. This 'Liberal Revolution' opened new chapter in Guatemalan history, bringing radical modernization reforms.

events.title: Justo Rufino Barrios President
events.description: Justo Rufino Barrios became president, implementing radical liberal reforms. Barrios was authoritarian modernizer determined to transform Guatemala into secular progressive state. He weakened Church, promoted education, built infrastructure and pushed coffee economy. Barrios called 'Reformer,' ruling 12 years, thoroughly transforming Guatemalan society.

events.title: Church Separation and Secularization
events.description: Barrios implemented thorough secularization reforms: expelled Jesuits and other religious orders, confiscated Church property, established civil marriage and divorce, secularized cemeteries, removed education from Church control. Religious freedom guaranteed, weakening Catholic Church's monopoly. These reforms provoked strong Church and conservative opposition, but changed Guatemala's church-state relations, establishing secular state.

events.title: Public Education System
events.description: Barrios established free compulsory public education system, trying to eliminate illiteracy and create modern citizens. Government built schools nationwide, taking education from Church. Education based on positivism and liberal ideas, emphasizing science and reason. But in rural areas, especially Maya communities, education system implementation limited, illiteracy rates remained high.

events.title: Forced Labor Laws
events.description: To support expanding coffee economy, Barrios government passed forced labor laws requiring indigenous people to work for coffee plantations. Maya forced to leave communities, labor in coffee farms, with meager wages and harsh conditions. These laws created near-serfdom system, enriching coffee elites but impoverishing Maya communities. Forced labor became foundation of Guatemalan economy in first half of 20th century.

events.title: Coffee Boom
events.description: Coffee became Guatemala's main export commodity, bringing economic prosperity. Pacific coast and western highlands transformed into coffee plantations. Coffee elites (finqueros) accumulated enormous wealth and political power, forming oligarchy. Coffee boom drove infrastructure construction, including railways and ports. But prosperity relied on exploitation of Maya labor, deepening social inequality. Coffee-dominated economy made Guatemala vulnerable to international price fluctuations.

events.title: Liberal Succession
events.description: After Barrios's death, series of liberal leaders continued his modernization policies, including Manuel Lisandro Barillas. Liberal reforms continued: secularization, infrastructure construction and coffee economy expansion. But political instability, frequent coups and assassination attempts. Liberal oligarchy consolidated control over politics and economy.

events.title: Barrios Unification War
events.description: Barrios attempted to forcibly rebuild Central American Federation through military force. He declared himself Supreme Military Commander of Central America, invading El Salvador. But other Central American nations united against Guatemalan hegemony. On April 2, 1885, Barrios fell in Battle of Chalchuapa in El Salvador. His death ended attempt to forcibly unify Central America, but Barrios left legacy of modernizing Guatemala.

events.title: Manuel Estrada Cabrera Takes Power
events.description: Manuel Estrada Cabrera became president after coup. Cabrera initially viewed as moderate liberal, but soon established dictatorship lasting 22 years until 1920. He continued coffee economy and modernization, but rule became increasingly brutal, using secret police, censorship and political assassination to suppress opposition.

events.title: United Fruit Company Entry
events.description: United Fruit Company (UFCO) began large-scale operations in Guatemala, receiving massive land concessions for banana cultivation. UFCO established banana plantations on Caribbean coast, controlling railways and ports. Company received enormous tax breaks and land rights. UFCO became 'state within state,' having huge influence on Guatemalan politics and economy. This opened banana republic era, US corporate interests dominating Central American politics.

events.title: War with El Salvador
events.description: Guatemala waged war with El Salvador and Honduras, Cabrera trying to install friendly regimes in neighboring countries. War attracted US and Mexican mediation. This demonstrated Guatemala's continued military ambitions in Central America, but also showed its inability to dominate region. War resolved through negotiation, maintaining status quo.

events.title: Earthquake Disasters
events.description: Series of strong earthquakes in 1917 and 1918 destroyed Guatemala City, causing tens of thousands of deaths and widespread destruction. Most of city's colonial and 19th century buildings destroyed. Reconstruction slow due to Cabrera government corruption and economic difficulties. Earthquake disasters increased discontent with Cabrera's rule.

events.title: Cabrera Overthrown
events.description: After 22 years of dictatorship, Manuel Estrada Cabrera overthrown following mass protests, strikes and military rebellion. Students, workers, merchants and officers united against dictator. National Assembly declared Cabrera insane, removing him. Cabrera's fall caused widespread celebration, viewed as hope for tyranny's end. But political instability continued.

events.title: Brief Democratization
events.description: After Cabrera's fall, Guatemala experienced brief political opening and democratic experiment. Unions, student organizations and political parties emerged. 1920 election considered Guatemala's first relatively free election in history. But this democratic spring was brief, soon replaced by new authoritarian rule. Coffee oligarchy and military maintained control over politics.

events.title: Ubico Dictatorship
events.description: Ubico established personal dictatorship, centralizing power and suppressing all opposition. He used secret police, spy networks and political assassination to eliminate enemies. Ubico built roads and infrastructure, improved fiscal management, but at human rights cost. He maintained close relationship with United Fruit Company, protecting US commercial interests. Ubico was particularly brutal toward Maya and working class, maintaining coffee elite rule.

events.title: Jorge Ubico Takes Power
events.description: General Jorge Ubico elected president in 1931 election, beginning another long dictatorship lasting 13 years. Ubico promised to restore order and economic stability, attracting elite support during Great Depression. He established efficient but brutal police state, personally controlling all aspects of government. Ubico worshipped Napoleon, viewing himself as Guatemala's savior.

events.title: Debt Peonage Abolished
events.description: Ubico abolished debt peonage system that plagued Maya communities for decades. But he replaced it with equally oppressive vagrancy law requiring landless peasants to work 150 days annually. This essentially new form of forced labor, forcing Maya to continue working in coffee plantations. Ubico's 'reform' actually consolidated exploitation system.

events.title: October Revolution Begins
events.description: Student and urban middle-class led protests and strikes began against Ubico dictatorship. 'June Uprising' inspired by martyrdom of teacher María Chinchilla, shot by military during protest. Mass civil disobedience forced Ubico to resign in July. But military triumvirate took over, attempting to maintain old order.

events.title: October Revolution Success
events.description: Officers, students and workers launched uprising, overthrowing military triumvirate. Young officers Jacobo Árbenz and Francisco Javier Arana led military rebellion, uniting with students and civilians. On October 20, revolutionary forces captured Guatemala City, with almost no bloodshed. This 'October Revolution' viewed as turning point in Guatemalan history, opening 'Guatemalan Spring' period of democracy and reform.

events.title: Juan José Arévalo Elected
events.description: Juan José Arévalo, educator returned from Argentine exile, elected president by overwhelming majority in Guatemala's first truly democratic election. Arévalo was moderate social democrat, inspired by Roosevelt's New Deal. He promised 'spiritual socialism,' focusing on education, health and social reform. Arévalo's election marked beginning of Guatemala's democratic experiment.

events.title: New Constitution
events.description: Guatemala promulgated progressive new constitution guaranteeing freedom of speech, assembly and labor rights. Constitution established social security system, protected worker rights, limited presidential terms. Constitution abolished forced labor, granted women voting rights (literate women). This was Guatemala's most progressive constitution in history, reflecting October Revolution's democratic ideals.

events.title: Labor Code
events.description: Arévalo government promulgated progressive labor code guaranteeing collective bargaining rights, strike rights and minimum wage. Code limited working hours, improved working conditions, established labor courts. These reforms legalized unions, granting workers unprecedented rights. But code didn't apply to agricultural workers (mostly Maya), reflecting reform limitations. Coffee elites and United Fruit Company strongly opposed these reforms.

events.title: Arana Assassination
events.description: Military leader Francisco Javier Arana was assassinated, triggering political crisis. Arana was conservative officer planning to run for president in 1950. His death sparked coup rumors and military tensions. Arévalo barely maintained control, but event showed revolution's fragility and threat from conservative officers.

events.title: Jacobo Árbenz Elected
events.description: Jacobo Árbenz Guzmán, 1944 revolution hero and Arévalo's Defense Minister, elected president in free election. Árbenz promised to deepen revolution into more profound social and economic reforms, especially land reform. His election marked Guatemalan Spring entering more radical phase. Árbenz was idealist determined to address Guatemala's deep inequality and poverty.

events.title: Cold War and Red Scare
events.description: Árbenz government accused by US of being communist for allowing Communist Party legal existence and implementing land reform. United Fruit Company lobbied US government, claiming Guatemala becoming Soviet bridgehead in Americas. Actually, Árbenz was nationalist reformer not communist, but in Cold War context, US viewed any social reform as communist threat. Eisenhower administration decided to overthrow Árbenz, CIA began plotting coup.

events.title: Land Reform Law
events.description: Árbenz promulgated Agrarian Reform Law (Decree 900), Guatemala's most radical social reform in history. Law confiscated unused large landholdings (over 90 hectares), compensating with government bonds, redistributing to landless peasants. Reform targeted large estates, including United Fruit Company's vast lands. By 1954, about 100,000 families received land. Reform aimed to create peasant middle class, break oligarchy land monopoly, modernize agriculture. But reform threatened coffee elites and US company interests, provoking strong opposition from conservatives and US.

events.title: Counter-Revolutionary Government
events.description: Castillo Armas established counter-revolutionary regime, reversing decade's democratic achievements. Land reform abolished, land returned to original owners including United Fruit Company. Unions banned, leftists and reformers imprisoned or exiled. Political parties outlawed, voting rights restricted. Thousands of peasants lost land. This opened Guatemala's 'White Terror' period, repressing Árbenz era supporters.

events.title: CIA Coup (Operation PBSUCCESS)
events.description: CIA-orchestrated coup overthrew Árbenz's democratically elected government. CIA trained and funded rebel army led by Carlos Castillo Armas, invading from Honduras. CIA used psychological warfare, false radio broadcasts and aircraft bombing to create panic. Facing military betrayal and US pressure, Árbenz resigned June 27 and went into exile. Coup ended Guatemalan Spring's decade-long democratic experiment, landmark event of US intervention in Latin America during Cold War. Coup had catastrophic long-term effects on Guatemala, paving way for decades of military dictatorship and civil war.

events.title: Castillo Armas Assassination
events.description: President Castillo Armas assassinated by palace guard in presidential palace, motive still unclear. His death triggered political crisis and power struggle. After chaotic period and electoral fraud accusations, General Miguel Ydígoras Fuentes became president in 1958. Political instability showed counter-revolutionary regime's lack of legitimacy.

events.title: Officer Uprising and Civil War Beginning
events.description: Young nationalist officers launched uprising against corrupt Ydígoras government and US control over Guatemala. Uprising failed, but surviving officers escaped to mountains, forming guerrillas. This marked beginning of Guatemalan Civil War, lasting 36 years, becoming one of Latin America's longest and bloodiest civil wars. Uprising inspired by Árbenz's overthrow and Cuban Revolution's success.

events.title: Guerrilla Movement Established
events.description: Former officers Luis Turcios Lima and Marco Antonio Yon Sosa established guerrilla organizations MR-13 and FAR (Rebel Armed Forces). Guerrillas operated in eastern and central mountains, inspired by Cuban Revolution. They sought to overthrow military regime, restore democratic reforms. Guerrilla movement attracted peasants, students and leftist intellectuals disappointed by 1954 coup.

events.title: Peralta Coup
events.description: Colonel Enrique Peralta Azurdia staged coup, overthrowing democratically elected president. Peralta established military government, suspending constitution. This marked beginning of direct military rule period, lasting about 20 years. Military regime used anti-communism as excuse to repress all opposition.

events.title: Julio César Méndez Elected
events.description: Julio César Méndez Montenegro elected civilian president in military-allowed election. But he was forced to reach secret agreement with military, allowing army autonomy to combat guerrillas. Despite being civilian, Méndez couldn't control military, becoming puppet of military violence. His presidency witnessed intensified counter-insurgency repression.

events.title: White Terror
events.description: Guatemalan army launched brutal counter-insurgency campaign against eastern guerrillas with US military advisor support. Army and paramilitary death squads used mass terror, killing thousands of civilians, including suspected guerrilla supporters, union members, students and leftists. Many kidnapped, tortured and 'disappeared.' These tactics effectively crushed eastern guerrilla movement, but at cost of massive human rights violations. White Terror established repression pattern that would repeat for decades.

events.title: Military Strongmen
events.description: 1970s ruled by series of military strongman presidents: Carlos Arana Osorio (1970-74), Kjell Laugerud García (1974-78) and Romeo Lucas García (1978-82). These generals came to power through electoral fraud, establishing corrupt dictatorships. They repressed political opposition, tolerated death squads, looted treasury. Despite nominally elected, these regimes essentially military dictatorships. 1970s violence escalated, death squads kidnapped, tortured and murdered union leaders, students, professors and political activists.

events.title: Guerrilla Movement Revival
events.description: New guerrilla organizations emerged, especially in Maya highlands. Guerrilla Army of the Poor (EGP) operated in K'iche' region, Revolutionary Organization of the People in Arms (ORPA) in western highlands. These new guerrillas established closer ties with Maya peasants, unlike 1960s mainly Ladino guerrillas. Guerrillas exploited anger over military repression, land dispossession and extreme poverty. By late 1970s, guerrilla movement stronger than ever.

events.title: Great Earthquake
events.description: Devastating 7.5 magnitude earthquake struck Guatemala, killing 23,000, injuring 77,000 and leaving over one million homeless. Earthquake destroyed vast rural areas, especially Maya highland communities. International aid poured in, but corrupt military government embezzled most reconstruction funds. Earthquake exposed Guatemala's deep poverty and inequality. Disaster sparked social organization and consciousness, peasants and Maya communities establishing cooperatives and mutual aid organizations. These organizations later became basis for social movements and guerrilla recruitment.

events.title: Panzós Massacre
events.description: Army massacred over 100 K'iche' Maya peasants in Panzós protesting land seizures. Massacre occurred in broad daylight, international condemnation. This was early sign of military systematic violence escalation against Maya communities. Panzós shocked nation, pushing many Maya to support guerrilla movement or social organizations.

events.title: Genocide
events.description: Guatemalan army launched systematic extermination campaign against Maya communities, civil war's bloodiest period. Under Romeo Lucas García and General Efraín Ríos Montt, army implemented 'scorched earth' strategy, destroying hundreds of Maya villages. Army massacred entire communities, including women, children and elderly, to eliminate actual or potential guerrilla support. Over 200,000 killed or 'disappeared,' mostly Maya civilians. 626 villages completely destroyed. Over one million displaced, becoming internal refugees or fleeing to Mexico. Army used rape, torture and public executions to create terror. This was one of 20th century Americas' worst human rights catastrophes.

events.title: Spanish Embassy Fire
events.description: Maya peasants and student activists occupied Spanish Embassy in Guatemala City, protesting military violence. Security forces attacked embassy, triggering fire that killed 39 people including protesters and embassy staff. Only one peasant survived, but he was later kidnapped and murdered. This tragedy attracted international attention to Guatemala's human rights crisis. Spain broke diplomatic relations with Guatemala. This massacre outraged Maya communities and international opinion.

events.title: Civil Patrols
events.description: Army forcibly established Civil Defense Patrols (PACs), forcing Maya men to join paramilitary organizations. Over one million men forced to join PACs, patrolling communities under military supervision, combating guerrillas, sometimes participating in massacres. Refusing to join meant accusation of being guerrilla and execution. PACs militarized Maya communities, forcing them to participate in repressing their own people, dividing communities. This was key element of army counter-insurgency strategy, aimed at controlling rural population.

events.title: Ríos Montt Coup
events.description: General Efraín Ríos Montt staged coup, overthrowing Lucas García. Ríos Montt was evangelical Christian, promising to eliminate corruption and defeat guerrillas. He implemented 'guns and beans' policy: providing food for government supporters, massacre for resisters. Ríos Montt intensified counter-insurgency, overseeing worst genocide atrocities. He framed conflict as holy war against communism. Despite anti-corruption claims, violence reached unprecedented levels.

events.title: Mejía Víctores Coup
events.description: General Oscar Humberto Mejía Víctores overthrew Ríos Montt. Mejía continued counter-insurgency war, but reduced most extreme atrocities. He began political opening process, preparing transition to civilian rule, partly due to international pressure and military belief that guerrilla threat diminished. But repression and death squad activities continued.

events.title: New Constitution and Democratic Transition
events.description: Guatemala promulgated new constitution, restoring civilian rule and democratic elections. Constitution established human rights ombudsman, guaranteed basic rights, limited military power (theoretically). This marked formal transition to democracy, ending direct military rule. But military retained enormous actual power and autonomy, continuing human rights violations with impunity.

events.title: Vinicio Cerezo Elected
events.description: Vinicio Cerezo Arévalo elected civilian president, first in 30 years. Cerezo was Christian Democratic Party candidate, promising human rights and democratic consolidation. But he was strictly limited by military, unable to prosecute past violations or end war. Death squads and disappearances continued, though somewhat reduced. Cerezo's presidency showed democratic transition limitations: civilian government but military still controlled security and faced impunity.

events.title: Esquipulas Peace Agreement
events.description: Central American presidents signed peace agreement in Esquipulas, laying framework for ending regional conflicts. Agreement pushed by Costa Rican President Oscar Arias, who received Nobel Peace Prize for it. Agreement promised democracy, reconciliation and stopping armed conflicts. Though implementation slow, Esquipulas process eventually led to Guatemala peace negotiations, ending civil war.

events.title: Peace Negotiations Begin
events.description: Guatemalan government began peace negotiations with guerrilla umbrella organization URNG (Guatemalan National Revolutionary Unity) under UN mediation. Negotiations slow and difficult due to mutual distrust and military resistance. But Cold War end, international pressure and war stalemate pushed peace process. Negotiations would last six years, finally reaching comprehensive peace agreement.

events.title: Jorge Serrano Elected
events.description: Jorge Serrano Elías elected president, promising to advance peace negotiations. Serrano was evangelical businessman, initially pushing negotiations forward. But his government was corrupt and unpopular. Facing criticism, Serrano attempted self-coup (autogolpe) in 1993, dissolving Congress and Supreme Court.

events.title: Serrano Self-Coup Failed
events.description: Serrano's self-coup failed under strong opposition from civil society, business community and international community. Military refused to fully support coup. Serrano forced to resign and flee abroad. National Assembly elected human rights ombudsman Ramiro de León Carpio as president to complete term. This crisis's peaceful resolution viewed as victory for Guatemala's democratic institutions.

events.title: Indigenous Rights Agreement
events.description: Government and URNG signed Agreement on Identity and Rights of Indigenous Peoples, recognizing Maya culture and rights. Agreement promised respect for Maya languages, culture, land rights and self-determination. This was important peace process milestone, first official recognition of Maya rights and genocide impacts. But implementing agreement would be long-term challenge.

events.title: Peace Accords Signed
events.description: Guatemalan government and URNG guerrillas signed final peace agreement in Guatemala City, formally ending 36-year civil war. Agreement included ceasefire, guerrilla disarmament, military reform, human rights commission, indigenous rights and socioeconomic reforms. War caused over 200,000 deaths, 45,000 disappearances, about 83% of victims were Maya. Peace agreement brought hope Guatemala could end violence, build democratic and just society. December 29 became national Peace Day. But implementing agreement would prove daunting challenge.

events.title: Bishop Gerardi Assassination
events.description: Human rights advocate Bishop Juan Gerardi murdered two days after releasing Historical Memory Recovery Project (REMHI) report documenting military atrocities during civil war. Gerardi bludgeoned to death in his garage. This assassination shocked nation, showing dangers still existed in peacetime. Eventually, officers and priest convicted, but case revealed corruption and collusion within military and Church. Gerardi became martyr for truth and justice.

events.title: Historical Clarification Commission Report
events.description: UN-backed Historical Clarification Commission (CEH) released report 'Guatemala: Memory of Silence,' documenting civil war violations. Report confirmed over 200,000 dead or disappeared, 93% of violations committed by military. CEH determined military committed genocide against Maya. Report detailed 626 village destructions and systematic torture, rape and disappearances. CEH also criticized US support for Guatemalan military. Report was Guatemalan history milestone, officially documenting terror and demanding justice and reparations. But implementing recommendations slow.

events.title: Referendum Failed
events.description: Referendum on ratifying peace agreement constitutional reforms failed, with low turnout and majority opposing. Reforms would have strengthened indigenous rights, limited military and reformed judicial system. Failure reflected public fatigue, right-wing opposition campaign and peace process disappointment. This was major setback for peace implementation, showing Guatemalan society deeply divided on how to move forward.

events.title: Alfonso Portillo Elected
events.description: Alfonso Portillo elected president, backed by retired General Efraín Ríos Montt's FRG party. Portillo promised reforms, even acknowledging military atrocities in civil war. But his government was corrupt, entangled with Ríos Montt's influence. Portillo's term saw peace agreement implementation stalled, corruption increased. He was later convicted for corruption.

events.title: Óscar Berger Elected
events.description: Óscar Berger elected president on anti-corruption platform. Berger was former Guatemala City mayor and businessman, promising to fight corruption and restore economic growth. His government pushed free market policies and free trade agreement with US. But inequality, poverty and violence continued plaguing Guatemala.

events.title: CICIG Established
events.description: UN and Guatemalan government established International Commission Against Impunity in Guatemala (CICIG), assisting investigation and prosecution of corruption and organized crime. CICIG authorized to work with Guatemalan prosecutors, investigating connections between state and criminal networks. CICIG became powerful tool against corruption, investigating politicians, judges, police and businessmen. In 12 years operation, CICIG helped expose dozens of corruption cases, including those involving presidents and business elites.

events.title: Álvaro Colom Elected
events.description: Álvaro Colom elected center-left president, promising social programs and poverty combat. Colom implemented conditional cash transfer programs and rural development projects. But his government also faced corruption allegations and increasing criminal violence due to drug trafficking and gang activity.

events.title: Otto Pérez Molina Elected
events.description: Retired General Otto Pérez Molina elected president after promising 'iron fist' against crime. Pérez was former military intelligence officer, playing role in 1980s counter-insurgency war. He promised to use military against drug gangs and violence. But his hardline policies failed to reduce violence, his government engulfed in corruption scandals.

events.title: Ríos Montt Genocide Trial
events.description: Efraín Ríos Montt tried in Guatemalan court for genocide against Ixil Maya during 1982-83. He was found guilty, sentenced to 80 years prison, becoming first former head of state convicted of genocide. This was historic verdict, delivering justice for victims. But ten days later, Constitutional Court overturned verdict on procedural grounds, ordering retrial. Retrial indefinitely postponed, Ríos Montt never tried again before dying in 2018. Nevertheless, trial was important milestone, breaking impunity, giving survivors chance to voice.

events.title: Corruption Scandal and Pérez Resignation
events.description: CICIG and prosecutors exposed massive corruption network 'La Línea' (The Line) involving President Pérez Molina, Vice President and senior officials, profiting millions from customs bribes. Scandal triggered mass protests, tens of thousands in plazas demanding Pérez resignation. Facing pressure, Vice President resigned and was arrested. In September, Congress stripped Pérez immunity, he resigned and was arrested. These events shocked Guatemala, showing CICIG's power and civil society mobilization.

events.title: Jimmy Morales Elected
events.description: Jimmy Morales, former comedian and political outsider, elected president in anti-corruption and anti-establishment wave. Morales's campaign slogan 'Neither Corrupt Nor Thief' contrasted with professional politicians' corruption. But soon, Morales himself and family faced corruption investigations. When CICIG investigated him, Morales turned against commission, finally terminating CICIG mandate in 2019, provoking international criticism.

events.title: Migrant Caravan
events.description: Thousands of Guatemalans joined migrant caravans heading to US, fleeing poverty, violence and lack of opportunities. Caravans crossed Mexico, attracting international media attention. This highlighted Guatemala's ongoing socioeconomic crisis, especially rural areas. Migration became central issue in US-Guatemala relations, Trump administration pressuring Guatemala to sign 'safe third country' agreement.

events.title: CICIG Terminated
events.description: Morales government terminated CICIG mandate, commission forced to leave Guatemala. Termination provoked international criticism and concerns about anti-corruption rollback. CICIG in 12 years helped expose and prosecute dozens of major corruption cases. But its investigations threatened political and economic elites, who lobbied to terminate commission. After CICIG departure, investigations and prosecutions of corruption networks sharply declined, impunity culture revived.

events.title: Alejandro Giammattei Elected
events.description: Alejandro Giammattei elected president, promising to combat corruption and crime, promote economic development. But his election dimmed by low turnout and widespread disillusionment. Giammattei was retired prison director and conservative, his government facing COVID-19 pandemic, hurricanes and economic crisis challenges.

events.title: Budget Protests
events.description: Congress passed controversial budget drastically cutting education and health spending while increasing lawmakers' allowances, triggering mass protests. Demonstrators occupied and burned part of Congress building. Protests reflected deep anger and frustration with political class. Facing pressure, Congress withdrew budget. Protests showed civil society still active post-CICIG, but also showed institutional dysfunction.

events.title: Attacks on Judicial Independence
events.description: Giammattei government and allies launched attack on judicial system, especially targeting anti-corruption prosecutors and judges. Attorney General replaced with government ally, dismissed several prosecutors investigating corruption. Judges investigating CICIG-related cases faced harassment and persecution. Many prosecutors, judges and activists forced into exile. This represented serious rollback of anti-corruption and rule of law, provoking international condemnation.

events.title: Bernardo Arévalo Elected
events.description: Bernardo Arévalo, former diplomat and social democratic candidate, elected president in surprising electoral victory. Arévalo was son of 1940s President Juan José Arévalo, representing Seed Movement party (Semilla). His campaign promised to fight corruption, restore democratic institutions and rule of law. Arévalo's election viewed as rejection of corrupt establishment, bringing hope to many Guatemalans. But post-election, prosecutors and establishment forces tried to block his inauguration, triggering political crisis.

events.title: Inauguration Crisis
events.description: After Arévalo's election, Attorney General and political elites tried to overturn election results, investigating Seed Movement party, attempting to cancel its legal status and block Arévalo's inauguration. This triggered mass protests and international pressure supporting democratic transition. Indigenous and peasant organizations blockaded roads demanding respect for election results. After months of tension, Arévalo finally inaugurated January 14, 2024, but facing continued opposition from Congress and judicial system. Crisis showed Guatemala democracy's fragility and elite resistance to reform.

events.title: Arévalo Presidency Begins
events.description: Bernardo Arévalo inaugurated president after obstacles, promising anti-corruption, restoring rule of law and addressing social inequality. Arévalo government faces enormous challenges: entrenched corruption networks, hostile Congress and judicial system, economic stagnation, extreme poverty (especially Maya communities), violent crime, drug trafficking and mass migration. He tries to restore anti-corruption institutions, hold abusers accountable, implement social reforms. But resistance from political elites and criminal networks is fierce. Guatemala remains deeply unequal and divided: small elite controls wealth and power, majority population lives in poverty. Over 50% of population poor, Maya communities most affected. Violence, insecurity and lack of opportunities continue driving migration. 1996 peace agreement promises mostly unrealized. But Arévalo's election also represents hope, democratic forces still exist, civil society mobilization can challenge impunity. Guatemala's future depends on breaking corruption and violence cycles, achieving true social justice, healing historical trauma of civil war and colonialism. This nation with rich Maya heritage and enormous potential stands at crossroads, struggling for democracy, justice and dignity.
